ideas.hypothesis: Pairwise co-mention intensity of firms on Twitter predicts the pairs' subsequent return co-movement beyond what shared SIC industry and shared headquarters city explain, and the incremental effect survives multi-factor controls.

sources.role: measure: news/forum-based relatedness of stock pairs explains comovement as well as SIC
method/finding: headquarters-city comovement shrinks with added pricing factors, showing need for factor controls and a proper null
method: distance-matrix approach for grouping stocks

ideas.test: Collect Twitter co-mention counts for S&P 500 firm pairs over one year; regress next-year pairwise daily return correlation (residuals from Fama-French plus industry factors) on co-mention intensity, same-SIC and same-HQ-city dummies, with pair-level controls for size and book-to-market similarity.
ideas.disconfirming: Co-mention intensity has no significant incremental association with residual correlation once SIC, HQ city and factor exposures are controlled, or its effect disappears out of sample.

ideas.hypothesis: High consumer confidence predicts lower medium-horizon (6-24 month) returns for small-cap stocks but not for large-cap stocks, because sentiment-driven retail demand concentrates in small firms and later reverses.

sources.role: finding: high consumer confidence followed by low returns; confidence tracks individual investor sentiment
finding/method: frequency-dependent effect, observed only for small-firm index; reverse causality

ideas.test: Monthly US data: regress future 1-, 6-, 12- and 24-month returns of size-sorted portfolios on the orthogonalized Michigan/Conference Board confidence index (purged of past returns and macro fundamentals), comparing small vs large decile coefficients with Newey-West errors.
ideas.disconfirming: Confidence coefficients for small and large caps are statistically indistinguishable, or the small-cap negative coefficient vanishes after purging lagged returns.

ideas.hypothesis: Momentum profits that are insignificant after CAPM/Fama-French adjustment become significant when restricted to stocks with high time-varying idiosyncratic volatility, reflecting limits to arbitrage rather than systematic risk.

sources.role: finding/method: TGARCH-M time-varying unsystematic risk helps explain momentum in Taiwan
setting/finding: momentum profitable in Shanghai after transaction costs, industry dependence
method: TGARCH parameter estimation for individual stocks

ideas.test: Using Taiwan or Shanghai monthly returns, estimate stock-level TGARCH conditional idiosyncratic volatility, double-sort into volatility terciles and past 6-month return quintiles, and compute transaction-cost-adjusted Fama-French alphas of winner-minus-loser portfolios per tercile.
ideas.disconfirming: Winner-minus-loser alphas do not rise with idiosyncratic volatility tercile, or high-volatility momentum alpha is fully absorbed by transaction costs.

ideas.hypothesis: The negative relation between dispersion in sell-side analyst recommendations and future returns appears only in high investor sentiment periods, when optimists set prices under short-sale constraints; in low-sentiment periods the relation is flat.

sources.role: measure/finding: disagreement among sell-side analysts, competing hypotheses that may neutralize each other
mechanism: investor sentiment changes as a channel to returns
measure: consumer confidence as sentiment proxy

ideas.test: Monthly cross-sectional regressions of next-month returns on recommendation dispersion (I/B/E/S), interacted with a high/low sentiment indicator (Baker-Wurgler or consumer confidence), controlling for size, book-to-market, momentum.
ideas.disconfirming: The dispersion coefficient is the same sign and magnitude in both sentiment regimes, or more negative in low sentiment.

ideas.hypothesis: Using a test robust to event-induced volatility, abnormal returns around hurricane landfalls are significantly negative for small firms in exposed industries but insignificant for large firms, and conventional tests overstate significance for large firms.

sources.role: finding/setting: negative returns around hurricane landfall, smaller impact on large firms
method: test for abnormal returns in small portfolios with event-induced volatility

ideas.test: Collect US hurricane landfall dates 1990-2019; form size-tercile portfolios of firms headquartered in affected states; compute abnormal returns with a standard Patell test and a volatility-adjusted test (e.g., BMP/variance-ratio), comparing results across size groups.
ideas.disconfirming: Size-group differences in abnormal returns are absent, or the volatility-robust test gives the same inference as the standard test.

ideas.hypothesis: Mood-related calendar effects (lunar-cycle and temperature effects) are larger in markets and stocks with higher retail investor trading shares.

sources.role: finding: new-moon vs full-moon return differences across 25 countries
finding/method: temperature effect in Thailand with AR-GARCH
setting: heavy flipping/turnover in Chinese retail-dominated market

ideas.test: For a panel of national indices, estimate lunar-phase return differentials with AR(1)-GARCH(1,1), then regress country-level effect sizes on retail share of trading volume; within China, compare the effect across stocks sorted by retail ownership.
ideas.disconfirming: No positive association between retail share and calendar-effect magnitude across countries or within-market sorts.

ideas.hypothesis: Stocks heavily bought by mutual funds with large inflows earn lower subsequent returns because flow-induced price pressure reverses over the following quarters, distinct from value and momentum effects.

sources.role: finding: negative relation between fund flows and stock returns, independent of value and momentum
method: De Bondt-Thaler winner/loser reversal framework

ideas.test: Compute stock-level flow-induced trading from quarterly fund holdings and flows (Chinese or US data); sort stocks into quintiles and track cumulative abnormal returns over the next 8 quarters, controlling for book-to-market and past returns.
ideas.disconfirming: High flow-pressure stocks show no positive contemporaneous return followed by reversal, or the pattern is explained by value/momentum factors.

ideas.hypothesis: Volatility-dynamics clusters (from TGARCH parameters and squared-return periodograms) identify groups of stocks among which volatility spillovers are significantly stronger than between clusters, improving out-of-sample covariance forecasts.

sources.role: method: TGARCH/spectral distance matrix and hierarchical clustering of DJIA stocks
method: VAR-based spillover analysis
mechanism: information demand drives volatility clustering

ideas.test: Cluster DJIA stocks using the 2000-2009 sample, then over 2010-2019 estimate pairwise volatility spillover indices (Diebold-Yilmaz) and compare within-cluster vs between-cluster averages; compare covariance forecast loss of cluster-block vs SIC-block shrinkage.
ideas.disconfirming: Within-cluster spillovers are not larger than between-cluster spillovers, or cluster-based covariance forecasts do not beat industry-based ones.

ideas.hypothesis: Changes in investor sentiment mediate the presidential-cycle return pattern more strongly in regions whose partisanship matches the incumbent's party, so local-firm returns rise more where residents are politically aligned with the president.

sources.role: mechanism/method: sentiment changes mediate political cycles and returns
mechanism: local investors and geographic variation in return relations
measure: headquarters-location-based local return comovement

ideas.test: Build state-level portfolios of locally headquartered firms; regress monthly portfolio returns on an alignment indicator (state's presidential vote share for incumbent party) and run a mediation analysis with state-level consumer sentiment changes, controlling for national factors.
ideas.disconfirming: Alignment has no effect on local portfolio returns, or sentiment changes do not mediate any of the alignment effect.

ideas.hypothesis: Modeling long memory in realized volatility (ARFIMA) yields a significantly positive risk-return tradeoff in emerging markets where short-memory GARCH-M estimates are insignificant or negative.

sources.role: method/finding: long-memory volatility with positive risk-return tradeoff and leverage effect
method: GARCH-M specification as comparison
method: nonparametric return distributions in Hang Seng to check fat-tail robustness

ideas.test: Using intraday data for Hang Seng and Shanghai indices, compute daily realized volatility, fit ARFIMA forecasts, and regress monthly excess returns on forecasted volatility; compare to GARCH-M estimates over the same sample.
ideas.disconfirming: ARFIMA-based volatility coefficients are no more positive or significant than GARCH-M coefficients.
